summary: Supply the league ERA, the league Home Runs, the league Walks and the league Hits by Pitch and the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator solves for strikeouts. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator work?
sections.html:
The FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports strikeouts in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (calculate Constant?); then you type in the league ERA, the league Home Runs, the league Walks and the league Hits by Pitch.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Strikeouts=(1 ÷ 2) × FIP constant × innings Pitched − 1 ÷ 2 × FIP × innings Pitched + (3 ÷ 2) × hits by Pitch + (13 ÷ 2) × home Runs + (3 ÷ 2) × walks
Constant=(league ERA × league Innings Pitched − 3 × league Hits by Pitch − 13 × league Home Runs + 2 × league Strikeouts − 3 × league Walks) ÷ league Innings Pitched
Constant=(FIP × innings Pitched − 3 × hits by Pitch − 13 × home Runs + 2 × strikeouts − 3 × walks) ÷ innings Pitched

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the league ERA, the league Home Runs and the league Walks — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns strikeouts, derived from the league ERA, the league Home Runs and the league Walks. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the league ERA, the league Home Runs, the league Walks and the league Hits by Pitch, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the FIP (Fielding Independent Pitching) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
